title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Project goal
To effect transformative change in wrack management globally. Our goal is to reduce conflict, improve transparency in beach management, and help managers align practices with biodiversity and climate goals while sustaining coastal tourism, economic, and community benefits.

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Motivation for the project
A significant, yet often overlooked, threat to beach biodiversity is the widespread practice removing wrack (washed-up kelp, seaweed, and seagrass) from beaches. Beach grooming is intended to improve the aesthetic quality of recreational beaches because of the social perception is that beaches should be ‘clean’. Wrack harvesting is removal of wrack for commercial purposes, such as making agar or providing feed in aquaculture.
These practices of removing wrack from beaches impact the natural system:

they remove food and habitat for invertebrate animals that depend on wrack, thereby impacting the survival of larger species such as seabirds
they reduce sand accumulation and dune formation, impacting the ecosystem service of coastal protection from large waves and storm

On the other hand, human activities can also cause excessive wrack accumulation through nutrient enrichment from agriculture and urban runoff. In such cases, beach cleaning may be necessary to reduce eutrophication impacts and can even enhance biodiversity.
A more nuanced understanding of these socio-ecological dynamics is therefore needed to support informed decisions about when beach cleaning is beneficial and when it is harmful to balance ecological, social and economic imperatives.



Wrack is beach-cast kelp, seaweed and seagrass. (Linda Harris CC-BY-NC)

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Objectives
The project is divided into six work packages that collectively:

Understand how perceptions, cultural norms and governance frameworks shape wrack-related decisions.
Identify which components of beach biodiversity depend on wrack, and how different wrack management regimes affect them.
Assess key ecosystem services linked to wrack (e.g., habitat support, coastal protection, nutrient and carbon cycling) and quantify trade-offs under alternative management options.
Co-develop and test practical interventions that can reconcile biodiversity outcomes with tourism and community needs, and deliver a Best Practice Guide and policy briefs for implementation.

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Project goal
To identify focus areas for beach conservation and build local capacity to have ‘beaches for life’ – in terms of biodiversity, human health and wellbeing, and for the long term – in southern and east Africa.
The study region will be used as a test area for developing innovative methods that will be scaled up to continental and global analyses, and the focus areas can be taken up by countries for implementation and further research.

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Motivation for the project
Sandy beaches are highly valuable ecosystems that contain a unique biota with high rates of endemism, support the life-history stages of many threatened focal species like shorebirds, turtles, horseshoe crabs, and provide two-thirds of all types of ecosystem services, including food for small-scale fishers, significantly more benefits for mental health than urban parks, and coastal protection against extreme storms and waves.
Unfortunately, high-value sea-facing real estate has been inappropriately developed too close to the shore. Beaches are now lined with seawalls, losing sand to widespread erosion and intense sand mining, and facing rising sea levels and increased storminess that are predicted to accelerate erosion.
This overlooked ecosystem is in a state of largely unnoticed crisis, and urgently needs action for change if we are to achieve the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity goals and targets for beaches, and maintain the benefits we derive from them for current and future generations. But expertise and science in sandy beach conservation to guide decision makers is extremely limited in Africa.

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Theory of change
The long-term goal is to have healthy, well-managed sandy beaches throughout the region that are intact, conserve unique biodiversity, contribute substantial ecosystem services to people, and are managed sustainably. This requires expertise in the respective countries in sandy beach ecology and conservation to advise decision-makers, and foundational information on beaches, their threat status, protection level, and where the priorities are for conservation (protection and restoration).
Beaches for Life! will address this by generating foundational knowledge, training a team of scientists per country, establishing a community of practice in beach conservation in southern and east Africa, and bringing those scientists into the global scientific community at the 10th International Sandy Beach Symposium in South Africa in 2027.

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Objectives
1. To develop an ecosystem classification and map for southern and east Africa through field sampling and remote mapping methods
2. To undertake ecosystem threat status assessment and protection level analysis
3. To identify focus areas for conservation of beaches
4. To build capacity and future leaders in sandy beach ecology in southern and east Africa

title: Citizen science
text:
If you have ever wanted to contribute to research and conservation, this is your chance! There are several citizen science projects on iNaturalist that you can join. It’s the perfect excuse to go to the beach!
Think of it as Instagram for nature. Go to the beach, take pictures of any plants or animals that you can find with the GPS of your phone turned on, post the pictures to the iNaturalist app (on the Apple and Play Stores) or the iNaturalist website, use the AI suggestions for the identification or give it your best guess, and you’re done. Other people will help to identify what you saw, and when enough people agree, the observation gets recorded as ‘Research Grade’.
You never know, you might just have found a species that no one knows about yet. Or found a species where it hasn’t previously been recorded. All observations count!
There are three beach projects you can contribute to…

1. Sandy Beaches (s Afr)


This project includes all observations of sandy beach macrofauna - the insects, crabs, snails, clams, sand piranhas, worms and other small invertebrate animals on beaches in southern Africa. Most of these species have very limited distributions and are often found in one bioregion, and no where else in the world! The best places to look for these animals is where the sand is wet on the beach, and under washed-up kelp, seaweed and damp driftwood.




    Latest observations. Explore all observations at
    
      Sandy Beaches (s Afr) »
    
  




2. Seashore Vegetation (s Afr)

 Dunes are the most sensitive component of sandy shores. The plants that grow on dunes are highly specialised, with pioneer species helping to bind sand together and promote dune formation. Dune plants sometimes require a salt crust on the surface of the sand so they can establish themselves and grow. The salt crust breaks when people walk on dunes, so if you’re taking pictures of dune plants, try to keep off the dune itself to protect these important plants.




    Latest observations. Explore all observations at
    
      Seashore Vegetation (s Afr) »
    
  




3. Ghost Crab Watch (s Afr)


With climate change, many species are shifting their ranges to move into climatic conditions that have become suitable for them, or move away from areas that are no longer suitable. Beach animals only have one choice - to move along the shore, so it’s reasonably easy to track shifts in their ranges. Ghost crabs are expanding their ranges along the South African south coast as the Agulhas Current warms, and the baby crabs are able to survive the cold winters.




    Latest observations. Explore all observations at
    
      Ghost Crab Watch (s Afr) »

Beaches provide important benefits to people, delivering two-thirds of all types of recognised ecosystem services, including every type of cultural service. All components of the littoral active zone (dunes, beach, surf) are important for delivering services in 11 ecosystem service bundles.
Read more








As ecotonal ecosystems at the land-sea interface, beaches are often poorly represented in ecosystem maps. We define a seashore zone from the dune base - as a proxy for the decadal scale high water mark - to the back of the surf zone, using remote methods to map ecosystem types therein.

title: Beaches are living ecosystems
text:
When we think about sandy beaches, the picture that usually comes to mind is sun-kissed holidays spent playing in the sand and surf, lying on a colourful beach towel under an umbrella reading or simply staring out at the waves, and cooling off periodically with a dip in the sea.
While you’re doing all that, under your beach towel there are about 70 animals (more in some places, fewer in others) that are buried in the sand. All we generally see is sand and surf, but beaches are living ecosystems, just like forests, reefs and mangroves, with predators and prey in constant pursuit.

title: Beaches are living ecosystems
section: Not all beaches are the same
text:
Not all beaches are the same
Beaches are shaped by sand, waves and tides. This means that unlike most ecosystems that are largely fixed by solid ground, rocks and plants, beaches are dynamic, continually shifting their form through processes of erosion - sand moving off the shore - and accretion - sand accumulating on the shore.



Erosion and accretion are a natural cycles that shape beach ecosystems. © Linda Harris


This constant movement of sand on and off the shore is why scientists prefer to define beaches in the context of the littoral active zone - the across-shore zone of sand within which sand is mobile. It comprises the foredunes, intertidal beach, and the surf zone. This distinction is important for how beaches are managed, but we’ll come back to that.



The littoral active zone, comprising the foredunes, beach and surf, is the zone within which sand is mobile. © Linda Harris


Even though beaches are dynamic ecosystems, there are still broad types of sandy shores that are recognised, with beaches tending to persist as a single type over time (unless there is a major disruption in the system). These types depend on the tide range, wave climate, and the local sand that get shaped into different forms. Scientists refer to these shore forms as beach morphodynamic types.

title: Beaches are living ecosystems
text:
Beach morphodynamic types
In microtidal climates where the tide range is less than 2 m, waves play a stronger role in shaping the beach than do the tides, and so they are considered to be wave-dominated beaches. In South Africa, all the beaches are microtidal.
Where the sand grain size is fine, the beach is wide and flat. The surf zone is usually wide too, with large waves that lose energy as they tumble through to the shore. These are called dissipative beaches.



Dissipative beaches are wide and flat with fine sand. © Linda Harris


Where the sand grain size is coarse, the intertidal beach is narrow and steep. The surf zone is usually narrow too, with waves that break often directly onto the shore, sometimes reflecting their energy back to sea and colliding with the next row of incoming waves. These are called reflective beaches.



Reflective beaches are narrow and steep with coarse sand. © Linda Harris


Between these two types are a range of intermediate beaches that have medium-grained sand, and moderate slopes and surf zones. Characteristic features of these beaches are usually well-formed rip currents and/or sand bars in the surf, and cusps - rolling hills of sand - along the shore.



Intermediate beaches usually have rip currents or sand bars in the surf, and cusps on the shore; look carefully to see the cusps on this beach. © Linda Harris


As the tide range becomes larger (>2 m) and larger (>4-6 m), beaches respectively become tide modified, and then tide dominated, as the role of tides shaping the shore increases. These kinds of conditions produce ultra-dissipative beaches and mud flats.
Think of the beaches you like to visit - what morphodynamic type do you think it is?

title: Beaches are living ecosystems
text:
Beach animals
When visiting the shore, you may have seen some crabs scuttle past, or a few snails crawling where the sand is wet. Although some animals are visible above the sand, most live their lives in the sand, some emerging to swim in the water as the tide comes in. The densities of animals buried in the sand depends on the beach morphodynamic type.
Living on a beach for a small animal (mostly 1 mm to 10 cm) is challenging because the world around them is constantly moving. It’s similar to what it would be like for us to live in a kids’ ball pit that is filled with balls and continually splashed with and submerged in water.



Living on beaches can be challenging if you’re a small animal, like this beach hopper, Africorchestia meridionalis. © Linda Harris


If the waves come fast, the animals have very little time to bury themselves. The grain size of the sand can also make that job harder. This is why beach morphodynamics plays such a critical role in shaping beach communities.
On dissipative beaches, the waves gently wash up onto the shore, usually spaced relatively far apart. This gives animals a good amount of time to bury themselves into the fine sand to avoid getting washed away. On reflective beaches, the short time between waves that hit the shore with more force makes it difficult to burrow into the coarse sand before the next wave washes them away.
Because reflective beaches pose harsher conditions for beach animals to survive, the number and types of animals is greater on dissipative beaches than on reflective beaches, and animal abundance and diversity on intermediate beaches falls somewhere in the middle.
Under the average beach towel, you can expect to find around 70 of these animals. But if you take a walk on a dissipative beach, within a 1-m strip of shore from the waves to the dunes, you can find up to 500 000 individuals of a single species!
Visit the Sandy Beaches (s Afr) project on iNaturalist to view some of the beach species that you can find in southern Africa, and Sandy Beach Invertebrates (Global) project to look for beach species found elsewhere in the world.
Next time you go to the beach, see if you can spot some of these interesting animals.

title: Beaches are full of life
text:
If asked to name animals that live on the beach, many would list turtles and perhaps some of the shorebirds - like seagulls, terns, sanderlings and plovers. Indeed, sea turtles lay eggs in carefully dug nests on beaches, and shorebirds feed and nest on beaches too. Although some of these vertebrate animals are found on beaches year-round, many are migratory species that use beaches seasonally. The biggest community of local residents are made up of invertebrate species - animals without a backbone.
Ranging in size from about 1 mm to 10 cm, there are hoards of macrofauna species that live on beaches year-round. These include surf shrimps, plough snails, clams, mole crabs (sea lice), worms, sand piranhas, beach hoppers, beetles, and roly-polies (pill bugs). Ghost crabs are probably the largely resident invertebrates on most beaches, with adults growing well over 10 cm in size if you include their legs in the measurement.

title: Beaches are full of life
text:
Adaptations for survival
Although it sounds idyllic to live on the beach, when you such a small animal, each wave is like a tsunami, threatening to wash them out to sea! If they remain on the surface of the sand, it can get incredibly hot in the midday sun (as many of us have experienced!). This is why most beach animals spend the majority of their lives buried in the sand.
Beach animals can burrow with different levels of ease and speed. Among the fastest burrowers are mole crabs (also known as sea lice, although they are crabs, not lice). If you’re able to catch one and place it down in the wet sand, it disappears in the blink of an eye. Others take longer to burrow, like the beetles, sand hoppers, and roly-polies (also known as pill bugs, although they are isopods, not bugs). If the animals live within reach of the waves, and their burrowing time is longer than the time between successive waves, they will be washed away and won’t be able to survive on that beach.
Beach animals must have a way to swim, surf, jump, run or crawl. The sand and surf is in constant motion, and beach animals need a way to ‘go with the flow’ to escape predators, and find food and mates. Plough snails use their large foot like a surf board to surf in the swash, and can also it to crawl on wet beach sand. Sand piranhas crawl on the sand, and are very fast swimmers, emerging out the sand to hunt when submerged by the incoming tide. Sand hoppers and pymy mole crickets hop or jump to move around, and ghost crabs can use their many legs to reach top speeds as they run across the shore.
Beach animals need to move with tides. To maintain their relative position on the shore, beach animals need to migrate across the shore with the tides, or else they must live in cycles where they are periodically submerged under water. Plough snails continually surf in the swash to ensure they stay in the dynamic wet edge of the sea. Clams also migrate with the tides, using the vibrations on the shore from breaking waves as a cue to emerge out the sand and surf using their foot, although much less efficiently than the plough snails because a clam’s foot is better suited to burrowing and anchoring in the sand.

title: Beaches are full of life
text:
Very specific habitats
Because beach animals have to be so specialised to deal with the dynamic physical environment around them, they tend to have very specific habitats in which they live. Most species live either on the low shore, midshore, high shore, or above the high-tide mark. They also tend to live on only one or two of the beach morphodynamic types, and in one or two biogeographic regions.
This means that many beach animals in South Africa are found only on our west (Southern Benguela), south (Agulhas) or east coasts (Natal-Delagoa), in a specific zone on a subset of the beaches in that region. These very specific habitat requirements makes them susceptible to impacts from a variety of pressures, like coastal development, mining, removing wrack (washed up kelp and seaweed) and pollution because they often can’t survive anywhere else than right where they are.
This also means the responsibility to look after many of the species is entirely up to us in South Africa because these animals occur here and nowhere else on earth.
Visit the Sandy Beaches (s Afr) project on iNaturalist to view some of the beach species that you can find in southern Africa, and Sandy Beach Invertebrates (Global) project to look for beach species found elsewhere in the world.
Next time you go to the beach, see if you can spot some of these interesting animals.
